notes.1a: The majority of candidates gained full credit for this question. Weaker candidates divided 200 by 50. Only a small number of candidates explained that average thickness equals total thickness divided by number of sheets.
notes.1b: The vast majority of candidates correctly calculated the density of iron. Weaker candidates inverted the equation and so divided 7.65 by 1377, or simply multiplied the two values together.
notes.1c: Candidates found this item challenging, with many giving answers such as “weighing scales” or “weighing meters”.
notes.2ai: The vast majority of candidates gained full credit.
notes.2aii: The vast majority of candidates identified the constant speed as 35 m / s.
notes.2b: Most candidates identified the car as slowing down, but few stated that the car became stationary.
notes.2c: Most candidates correctly calculated the area under the graph to give a distance of 700 m. The most common mistakes were to either attempt to find the area under the whole graph, or to use the wrong time interval. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2021
notes.2d: The vast majority of candidates correctly calculated the average speed of the car as 7.5 m / s. Weaker candidates usually multiplied the two values together.
notes.3a: Most candidates correctly evaluated the moment of the weight of the beam as 270 N m. The most common error was giving the unit as N / m. Weaker candidates divided 150 by 1.8.
notes.3b: Only stronger candidates were able to answer this question fully correctly.
notes.4a: Many candidates gained partial credit, but only the strongest candidates gained full credit. The most common errors involved failing to identify the transfers of energy and linking them to different parts of the motion.
notes.4b: The majority of candidates identified that some of the energy had been transferred but failed to state the form to which it was transferred or failed to identify the mechanism of transfer.

notes.5aii: Very few candidates correctly evaluated the gas pressure as 89 common error was to either add or subtract 7 from the value for atmospheric pressure.
notes.5b: The majority of candidates scored at least partial credit. Very few candidates stated that pressure = force ÷ area, but the concept that a small surface area produces a large pressure on the ground was well understood.
notes.6ai: The vast majority of candidates correctly stated that the temperature indicated on the thermometer was 32 °C.
notes.6aii: 1. Candidates found it challenging to explain that the reason for the thin glass bulb was to enable the rapid transfer of thermal energy to the liquid in the bulb. 2. Candidates also found it difficult to explain that the narrow capillary would give a large movement of mercury along the capillary for a small change in temperature.
notes.6b: Most candidates gained at least partial credit for this question. The most common error was failing to draw a horizontal section to represent the freezing of the liquid.
notes.7ai: The majority of candidates correctly identified X-rays, but a number could not identify ultraviolet as the other missing region.
notes.7aii: Most candidates identified a suitable use of gamma-rays. The most common errors were either to be too vague, e.g. “medical uses”, or to describe the use of X-rays in hospitals.
notes.7aiii: Very few candidates gained full credit. The majority of candidates thought that gamma-rays would travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum, with explanations such as “they have a shorter wavelength”.
notes.7bi: The vast majority of candidates answered this well but some could only be awarded partial credit as answers were not precise enough.
notes.7bii: Very few candidates stated that frequency was equal to the number of waves/pulses per second. Only stronger candidates gained full credit here. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2021
notes.8ai: The majority of candidates were able to draw a correct normal at X.
notes.8aii: Many candidates found this question difficult, with only a minority correctly labelling the angle of refraction.
notes.8aiii: The majority of candidates identified a correct piece of equipment. Weaker candidates gave answers such as “a ray of red light”, which failed to score.
notes.8b: Many candidates found this question challenging. The majority of candidates drew a ray of red light being refracted into the air. Many of those who drew a reflected ray failed to do so with adequate precision to score full credit.
notes.9ai: The majority of candidates identified the particles as electrons. Common errors included “protons” or just “electricity”.
notes.9aii: The majority of candidates identified the variable resistor. The most common error was to omit “variable”.
notes.9aiii: The majority of candidates correctly evaluated the resistance of the LDR as 110 Ω . Weaker candidates either inverted the equation or had a power of 10 error.
notes.9b: Many candidates gained credit for stating the current increased but failed to link this to a decrease in the resistance of the LDR.
notes.10ai: This topic was well understood, with the vast majority of candidates scoring at least partial credit. Weaker candidates gave suggestions such as “increasing the length of the coil”, or “changing the resistance of the coil”.
notes.10aii: Very few candidates linked the change in direction of rotation of the coil to reversing the direction of current in the coil.
notes.10b: Almost all candidates gained full credit for this question.
notes.11a: The majority of candidates were awarded partial credit for this question. The most common error was to state that A is the neutron number rather than the nucleon number.
notes.11bi: Most candidates were also awarded partial credit for this question. The most common error was failing to link the halving of the activity of the radioactive nuclide to its half-life.
notes.11bii: Many candidates gained at least partial credit here. The most common error was to divide the change in activity by 10, and then use 6000 in their estimation. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2021
